title: Edison Didn't Invent the Light Bulb #shorts
description:
Thomas Edison is famous for inventing the light bulb in 1879. He didn't — but he did make it practical.

Humphry Davy demonstrated electric arc light in the early 1800s, dozens of inventors built bulbs, and in England Joseph Swan showed one before Edison. The problem was they burned out fast. Edison's team tested thousands of materials; their carbon filament lasted much longer, and later bamboo bulbs passed 1,000 hours. Edison also built the whole system — power stations, wires and meters. He sued Swan, then the two teamed up as Ediswan.

Animated, voiced and scored in code. Narration is a synthetic (text-to-speech) voice.

title: Slaves Probably Didn't Build the Pyramids #shorts
description:
The pyramids are often pictured being built by armies of slaves. The evidence points to organised, fed and cared-for crews.

In 1990 archaeologists found the workers' tombs right next to the pyramids at Giza — an honour slaves would be unlikely to get. Some tombs held bread and beer for the afterlife, skeletons show healed broken bones, and nearby was a whole workers' town with bakeries, breweries and plenty of meat. Crews even named themselves, like "Friends of Khufu". Many worked rotating shifts and some were probably drafted labour — but slaves are unlikely. The slave image comes from ancient Greek writers and Hollywood.

title: Romans Didn't Have Vomit Rooms #shorts
description:
A vomitorium wasn't a room where Romans threw up so they could keep feasting. It was a corridor.

In amphitheatres and stadiums like the Colosseum, vomitoria were the passages that "spewed out" the crowds, letting tens of thousands of people leave in minutes — modern stadiums still use them. The myth comes from the word sounding like "vomit", and twentieth-century writers ran with it. Some Romans did overeat and throw up, apparently, but there was no special room.

title: Betsy Ross Probably Didn't Sew the First American Flag #shorts
description:
The story says George Washington visited Betsy Ross's shop in 1776 and asked her to sew the first flag. There's no record of that from the time — no letters, diaries or receipts.

The story first went public in 1870, almost 100 years later, told by her grandson from family stories. Betsy Ross was real: an upholsterer who did make flags, and in 1777 she was paid for ships' colours. But who designed the first flag is unclear; Francis Hopkinson billed the government for designing it and was never paid.
